tagline: Black asphalt replaced red cinder, but the coastal road kept its name.
intro: Route 137 follows Hawaiʻi Island’s eastern coast between Kapoho and Kalapana, beside the Pacific and the flat flanks of Kīlauea. The designated scenic byway offers ocean vistas and passes lava fields and protected areas, including Isaac Hale Beach Park. Sections wind along ocean cliffs and through tropical rainforest, with tree canopies of kamani, milo and hala. The route also carries the names Beach Road and Kapoho-Kalapana Road.

The Red Road’s name outlasted its surface. Long paved with volcanic red cinder, most of the road received black asphalt in 2000. Lava has made larger changes. The 1990 flow that destroyed Kalapana moved along the highway, and the 2018 eruption buried a section between Kamaili Road and Pohoiki Road and cut more of the route near Kapoho.

From the Kapoho end, the coastal sequence leads toward Isaac Hale Beach Park at Pohoiki Road, then MacKenzie State Recreation Area and Seaview, where Route 137 follows the Pacific shore. Kalapana lies southwest of Seaview. There, the 1990 flows destroyed most of the town and buried neighboring Kaimū and its bay beneath more than 50 feet of lava. The same eruption created a new coastline.

moments.title: Kapoho
moments.text: Kapoho was rebuilt after lava destroyed the town in 1960, becoming a community of private homes and vacation rentals. Lava destroyed it again in 2018. That second disaster changed the coast as well as the settlement. On June 4, lava entered Kapoho Bay; over the following days, it filled the bay. Nearby Green Lake had already disappeared on June 2, when lava boiled away its water and filled the basin. The Cape Kumukahi lighthouse survived the 1960 flow east of town, although the keeper’s dwellings were destroyed. The light continues in operation.

moments.title: MacKenzie State Recreation Area
moments.text: Ironwood trees connect this coastal park to the ranger who planted them. Albert J. MacKenzie established the grove in the 1930s; the park took his name after his death in 1938. A hiking trail follows the old Hawaiian coastal path called the King’s Highway, passing lava-tube mouths. The shore has rocks and cliffs, and the lava tubes open toward the ocean. The park forms part of the Malama Ki Forest Reserve. In May 2018, approaching lava flows prompted the park’s closure as lava entered the ocean at two nearby locations.

moments.title: Kalapana
moments.text: The coastline at Kalapana changed in 1990, when Kīlauea lava destroyed and partly buried most of the town. Nearby Kaimū and Kaimū Bay lie beneath more than 50 feet of lava. One building escaped by moving. Congregants strapped the Star of the Sea Painted Church to a trailer and relocated it just ahead of the advancing flow. Built in 1927–1928, the wooden church contains interior paintings by Father Evarist Gielen. It now stands on Highway 130 between mile markers 19 and 20. Gielen used housepaints and linseed to depict Bible stories and Hawaiian and Catholic history on the interior walls.

practical: Kapoho: In 2018, lava buried Route 137 between Kamaili Road and Pohoiki Road and cut additional sections near Kapoho. (checked 2026-10-11)
